candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Determine a common denominator and rewrite fractional parts as equivalent fractions before subtraction when denominators do not already match.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts use essentially the same name and definition for creating equivalent fractions with a shared denominator before subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite a whole number or mixed number into a subtraction-ready form, such as expressing a whole as a whole plus zero fraction or converting a mixed number with an improper fractional part into a standard mixed number.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A, B, and C all describe the same preparatory rewriting step for whole numbers and nonstandard mixed numbers before subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract fractional quantities once they are in compatible form, including subtracting numerators over a common denominator or subtracting fraction parts within mixed-number expressions.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: Expert C separates fraction-part subtraction into its own skill, while A and B fold this operation into a broader 'subtract aligned parts' skill that also includes whole-part subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract the whole-number components of mixed numbers or rewritten whole-number expressions as a distinct operation from fraction subtraction.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: Expert C explicitly isolates whole-number subtraction, whereas A and B include whole-part subtraction inside their broader aligned-subtraction skill.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract fractions with a shared denominator and/or subtract the whole-number parts once the quantities are in compatible form.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: Experts A and B define a combined subtraction skill covering both fraction-part and whole-part subtraction after setup; Expert C splits this broader concept into two separate skills (C03 and C04), so no single C skill is equivalent to the full combined concept.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Regroup one whole as an equivalent fraction and adjust the whole-number part when the fractional subtraction would otherwise be negative.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts describe the same regrouping/borrowing operation from the whole part into the fractional part during mixed-number or whole-minus-fraction subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Reduce the computed result to lowest terms or to an integer when the fractional part is reducible or equals zero.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A and B treat simplification as a separate post-subtraction skill. In C, simplification is merged with final expression into one combined skill rather than isolated.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Combine the computed whole and fractional parts and express the answer in an appropriate final form such as a mixed number, fraction, or integer.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A and B separate final recombination/presentation from simplification. C does not isolate this step and instead combines it with simplification in a single skill.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Reduce the computed result to lowest terms and present it in an appropriate final form such as a fraction, mixed number, or integer.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: Expert C combines two concepts that A and B keep separate: simplification and final expression of the answer.

alignment_summary: The three codebooks align strongly on common denominator, normalization, and borrowing/regrouping. The main structural differences are that Expert C splits 'subtract aligned parts' into separate fraction-part and whole-part subtraction skills, while Experts A and B keep them combined; conversely, Expert C combines simplification and final expression into one skill, while A and B separate those into two skills. Every skill_id from all three experts has been mapped exactly once.
